scope: Research-only evidence on agricultural structure, strategic value chains, market dependence, seasonal and food-security risks, and source availability. Not a farm-profit calculator profile and not authorization to activate Djibouti.

currency.name: Djiboutian franc
currency.note: Currency identification only. No dated, verified crop farm-gate prices or farm input quotations have been entered in this evidence file.

context.agroecology: Arid to hyper-arid environment with severe water scarcity, limited arable land, variable rainfall and soil salinity constraints. Production is concentrated in irrigated horticulture and arboriculture along watercourses and in selected protected/controlled environments; pastoral livestock is a major rural livelihood.
key_geographies: Djibouti City and surrounding horticultural supply areas
context.caution: Do not apply national averages uniformly across regions. Water access, irrigation energy, salinity, market distance, security and livestock mobility are material determinants of enterprise costs and yields.

evidence.topic: Recent national agricultural policy and value-chain priorities
evidence.source: World Bank Group, AgriConnect and Djibouti: Creating jobs and boosting food security in a resource-constrained region
observations: The World Bank reports that Djibouti imports about 90 percent of its food.

Agriculture contributes approximately 4 to 5 percent of GDP, while water and arable land scarcity, low and erratic rainfall, climate shocks, limited finance and weak market connections constrain producers.
Livestock accounts for approximately three-quarters of agricultural GDP, according to the article.
The Port of Djibouti livestock terminal handled more than 1.2 million animals in 2024 while operating at less than 20 percent of capacity.
The terminal throughput is a trade/transit statistic and must not be represented as the number of animals raised domestically.
Local horticultural production meets approximately 10 percent of demand; vegetable imports exceeded USD 35 million in 2021.
The article cites tomato yields up to 300 tonnes/ha under greenhouse cover and 40 tonnes/ha in open fields as production potential/illustrative benchmarks, not measured national average yields.
Djibouti produces about 110 tonnes of dates annually and imports roughly 2,300 tonnes; the plan aims for 5,850 tonnes after 2030.
evidence.caveat: Strategic-sector and market-context figures in a World Bank policy article, not a national agricultural census or farm survey. The tomato figures are illustrative attainable-yield examples and must not be used as guaranteed calculator yields. Livestock terminal throughput includes transit animals.

evidence.topic: Recent food and agricultural market structure
evidence.source: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, GAIN report DJ2026-0001, Djibouti Food and Agricultural Market Snapshot
observations: USDA FAS reports that nearly 90 percent of Djibouti's food supply is imported because of the arid climate, limited arable land and constrained domestic agricultural production.
The report identifies demand from supermarkets, hotels, restaurants, institutional buyers, military facilities and expatriate communities.
Port, free-zone and regional transport infrastructure support food distribution, cargo consolidation and re-export opportunities.
evidence.caveat: The landing page summary provides market structure and trade context, not domestic producer prices, production costs or farm-level gross margins. The attached full report should be reviewed for any additional product-specific import and market details before commercial use.

evidence.topic: 2026 acute food insecurity and pastoral livelihood risk
evidence.source: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), Djibouti: Acute Food Insecurity Situation May-June 2026 and Projection for July-December 2026

observations.indicator: Population in IPC Phase 3 or above, July-December 2026
Population in IPC Phase 3 or above, May-June 2026

observations_text: IPC identifies price shocks linked to import dependence, low purchasing power and strong El Niño conditions as drivers of worsening food insecurity.
Rural Tadjourah and rural Obock deteriorated to IPC Phase 4 in the July-December projection.
IPC recommends protecting agropastoral livelihoods through animal health, feed and water support, prioritising Obock, Dikhil and Tadjourah.
evidence.caveat: These are food-security classifications and projections, not agricultural production or farm profitability statistics. Keep observed classifications and projected populations explicitly distinguished.

evidence.source: FEWS NET, Djibouti Weekly Staple Food Price Data
observations: FEWS NET states that weekly Djibouti staple-food price data have been collected since 2004.
The page provides downloadable XLSX, CSV and JSON formats.
evidence.caveat: This is a useful time-series source for staple-food market/consumer prices, but the landing page alone does not establish the current latest observation, market coverage, commodity unit or farm-gate status. The dataset must be downloaded and its metadata and individual observations checked before any prices are quoted. Retail/market prices must not be relabelled as farm-gate prices.

evidence.source: FAO GIEWS Country Brief on Djibouti
observations: FAO reported that the March-May 2025 diraac/sougum rainy season performed poorly in inland pastoral areas of Dikhil, Obock and Tadjourah, with cumulative rainfall estimated at about 50 percent below average.
FAO noted reduced rangeland regeneration, pasture and water availability, with negative effects on livestock body condition.
Between October 2024 and May 2025, the national average wheat-flour price rose about 10 percent; the May 2025 price was about 7 percent below the year-earlier level.
The national average rice price declined about 8 percent between August 2024 and May 2025; in May 2025 it was about 5 percent below the year-earlier level.
evidence.caveat: Historical 2025 seasonal and consumer-price observations. These percentage changes are not absolute price levels, do not identify producer prices and must not be presented as current 2026 quotations.

evidence.topic: Agricultural production constraints and fertilizer context
evidence.source: French Treasury Directorate General, L'accès aux engrais à Djibouti

observations.source_note: Attributed by the Treasury note to Djibouti's national statistics institute.
Historical structural estimate quoted in the 2024 note.
Approximate national context figure in the note; spatial and interannual variation is substantial.
Historical estimate attributed to World Bank 2021 in the 2024 note.

observations_text: The note describes horticulture and arboriculture along watercourses as important forms of crop production.
It identifies water access and irrigation, rather than fertilizer availability alone, as critical constraints.
It describes limited farmer organisation, extension, finance, marketing services and cold-storage infrastructure as additional constraints.
It warns that large fertilizer import values passing through Djibouti largely reflect re-export to Ethiopia, not domestic fertilizer consumption.
evidence.caveat: These are historical 2019/2020 and earlier estimates quoted in an April 2024 policy note, not current 2026 production statistics. The USD 579.3 million fertilizer imports in 2022 were largely re-export flows and must not be used as a measure of Djiboutian farm input use.

evidence.source: FAOSTAT, Crops and livestock products dataset catalogue
observations: FAOSTAT provides annual country-level series for crop production, harvested area and yield, with coverage stated through 2024 in the dataset metadata.
FAO metadata notes that country data may originate from official statistics, surveys, administrative records or estimates based on expert observations.
evidence.caveat: A country/crop extraction for Djibouti, including metadata and flags, is still required. Do not treat all FAOSTAT values as direct survey observations without checking their source flags and estimation status.

data_quality_and_use: Djibouti's agricultural economy is structurally constrained by water scarcity, aridity, limited arable land and high dependence on imported food.
Livestock is a major rural livelihood and value chain, but livestock transit at the port must not be confused with domestic herd size or local animal production.

Horticulture, protected cultivation, water-efficient irrigation and dates are identified as strategic domestic value chains; their commercial viability depends heavily on water, energy, infrastructure, market access and buyer relationships.
The World Bank's greenhouse and open-field tomato yield figures are illustrative production potential, not verified national averages or guaranteed outcomes.
FEWS NET offers a long-running weekly staple price dataset, but prices must be downloaded and classified by market, date, commodity, unit and retail/wholesale/farm-gate status before use.
The current sources do not establish complete, current farm-gate price series or enterprise budgets for Djibouti.
The latest IPC projections show material food-security and pastoral risks in 2026; these should inform risk context but are not a substitute for agronomic data.
missing_data_before_calculator_use: A verified, current agricultural census or national farm survey with producer counts, farm sizes, irrigation area, crop areas and livestock populations by region.
FAOSTAT country-level extraction for the major crops and livestock commodities through 2024, with source flags and methodological notes.

District/market-specific dated producer prices for tomatoes, onions, other vegetables, dates, milk, meat, live animals and fodder, with grade, unit and explicit farm-gate/wholesale/retail classification.
Download and inspect FEWS NET weekly staple-price CSV/XLSX/JSON to extract current market observations, commodities, locations, units and dates.

Current farmer-paid costs for water, pumping, electricity/fuel, greenhouse structures and repairs, seed/seedlings, fertilizer, crop protection, labour, land preparation, packaging, cooling, storage and transport.
Crop-specific yields and crop cycles under open-field, greenhouse and other protected production systems, separated by location, water source, salinity, season and management level.

Livestock herd and flock inventories by species and production system; animal purchase/sale prices; feed, water, veterinary, labour, transport and mortality costs; and reproductive/productivity parameters.
Validation of dates production, horticulture market-share estimates and livestock value-chain indicators against underlying ministry or statistical publications.
Buyer contracts, farm-gate price deductions, quality grades, post-harvest losses, marketable yields and realistic financing costs for the selected value chains.
recommendation: Retain Djibouti as research-only. The strongest current evidence supports a livestock-led rural economy, a limited but strategically important irrigated/protected horticulture sector, date production potential, high import dependence and significant 2026 pastoral/food-security risks. Do not activate a calculator profile or use illustrative tomato yields as expected farm performance until current crop-level yields, local farm-gate prices and full water/energy/input/labour budgets are verified.
